title: The Potter and the Clay
overview: Watching a potter rework spoiled clay, Jeremiah learns that a nation's future can still change, but Judah refuses to change and plots against him.

parts.label: At the potter's wheel (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Jeremiah watches a potter shaping clay on a wheel, likely two round discs, one turned to spin the other. When a pot goes wrong, the potter does not throw the clay away but reshapes it into something else.

parts.label: What the clay means (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: God says Israel is like clay in his hands, but the lesson runs both ways: a nation warned of disaster can be spared if it turns from wrong, and a nation promised good can lose it if it turns to wrong. The future described is real but not locked, because it responds to how people act.

parts.label: A warning, and a refusal (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: God tells Judah that disaster is being shaped against them, yet urges each person to change course while there is still time. Jeremiah predicts their answer: it is hopeless, and they will keep following their own stubborn plans.

parts.label: Leaving the reliable for the worthless (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: The snow on Mount Lebanon and its cold streams never fail, yet the people have dropped their God for idols, leaving the old well-trodden roads for rough side tracks. The result will be a ruined land that passersby shake their heads at in shock and scorn, and God will turn his back on them as they turned theirs on him.

parts.label: The plot against Jeremiah (v. 18)
parts.note: His opponents decide they can do without him, since they still have priests to teach, wise advisers to counsel, and other prophets to speak. They plan to attack him with words, probably accusations, and ignore everything he says, though the exact sense of their reasoning is debated.

parts.label: Jeremiah's angry prayer (vv. 19-23)
parts.note: Jeremiah reminds God that he once pleaded for these people, then asks for famine, war and death on them and their families, and no forgiveness. It is one of the harshest prayers in the Bible; some read it as a prophet announcing a judgment already decided, while others see the raw cry of a hunted man, recorded honestly rather than offered as an example.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether God truly changes course in response to what people do, as verses 7 to 10 seem to say, or whether 'relenting' is a human way of describing a God whose plans never change.
think: When someone warns you that the path you are on will end badly, what makes it easier or harder to change course instead of digging in?
